item.title: What Grief Can Teach Us, If We're Willing to Listen
item.description:
Grief

What Grief Can Teach Us, If We're Willing to Listen

Why core emotions matter.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Grief is one of several core emotional systems wired into every mammalian brain.
  • We're built to heal grief in connection with others, not by processing it alone.
  • Numbing grief dulls joy too — the same circuitry carries both, so suppressing one mutes all.
Nan and Jilly Dog happy together
Source: Photo by Nan Wise

A few weeks back, my husband walked into our vet's office carrying a box of things we no longer needed — the little foam steps, the puppy pads, the small accommodations we'd built around our Chihuahua Jilly's failing heart, which finally gave out. He was there to donate them to another family who might need them.

He came home and said the front-desk staff cried when they saw the box. These are people who see loss every week. It's part of the job. And still, holding Jilly's steps in their hands, something in them broke open too.

I've been sitting with that moment ever since — not just as a story about losing my dog, but as a window into something much bigger: one of the ancient, hard-wired emotional operating systems that run underneath everything we call feeling. This is where my work keeps landing lately. Not "why does loss hurt?" but "why do we have a system built to make it hurt, and what happens when we stop listening to it?"

The System Has a Name

Affective neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp spent his career mapping the core emotional circuits shared across the mammalian brain — not learned habits, but hardware, built into the basement level of what I call the three-story brain. Care is the circuit responsible for bonding and attachment. Panic/Grief is the circuit that fires when an attachment bond is severed. It shares neurochemistry with physical pain, overlapping with the brain's opioid and oxytocin pathways — which is part of why grief is felt so viscerally in the body: the throat tightness, the ache in the chest, the bone-deep exhaustion no amount of sleep touches. I have been experiencing this acutely since Jilly’s passing. I miss her terribly. (Click here for tips to navigate grief).

I keep coming back to Panksepp's systems in my work because they explain so much more than any single life event. Seeking, Care, Panic/Grief, Play, Fear, Rage, Lust — these circuits don't just light up around sex, or around loss, or around any one domain of life. They're the operating system underneath it all. Grief is one of the clearest, least deniable demonstrations of a core system doing exactly what it evolved to do, which is why it makes such a good teacher. The lesson is about what happens when we misread any core emotional signal, including grief.

The Ache Is Information, Not Malfunction

Here's where our culture gets it backward. We've built an entire world around the premise that difficult feelings are problems to be solved, medicated, distracted from, or optimized away — scroll past it, numb it, reframe it into a productivity lesson before you've let yourself feel it at all. I call this collective habit the "Traumademic": a culture so saturated with unprocessed feeling that it treats all strong emotion, even entirely appropriate emotion, as something to numb or avoid rather than something to move through.

Panksepp saw the strength of a Panic/Grief response as a direct measure of how much the bond mattered in the first place. The intensity isn't dysfunction. It's the system reporting, with total accuracy, on the size of what it lost. That's true whether the bond was a seven-pound dog, a marriage, a friendship, or a version of yourself you had to let go of. Learning to read a core emotional signal instead of silencing it is one of the most useful skills a person can build — and it's a skill that transfers across every one of these circuits, not just this one.

We Were Never Built to Regulate Alone

Panksepp's research also found something gentler: comfort and social contact directly downregulate the Panic/Grief system. Touch, presence, and reunion soothe separation distress at a neurochemical level — not as a distraction from the pain, but as an actual intervention in it. No core emotional system is designed to be run in isolation. Care and Panic/Grief are wired to be navigated through connection, which is why the Traumademic's instinct to privatize every difficult feeling—to mute grief and keep it out of view — works against our own biology.

If you've ever lost a pet, you've experienced disenfranchised grief: a core emotional response our culture doesn't fully authorize. Studies comparing grief after pet loss to grief after human loss have found no significant difference in overall severity — the strength of the bond, not the species of the one we lost, predicts how hard the system fires. When my husband's story reached that vet staff and cracked something open in them, too. That was Care and Panic/Grief doing exactly what they evolved to do: resolving in the presence of someone else's nervous system.

You Cannot Selectively Numb a Core System

Here's what I think matters most, and what pet loss happens to illustrate with unusual clarity: the capacity to feel loss and the capacity to feel joy run through overlapping circuitry. A nervous system trained to shut down Panic/Grief doesn't get to keep an open channel to Seeking, to delight, to arousal, to awe. You cannot dampen one core emotional frequency and expect the others to play at full volume. This is the real argument underneath healthy hedonism — it was never just about chasing more pleasure. It's about protecting the full bandwidth of the operating system, which necessarily includes the circuits that hurt.

Why This Matters Beyond Grief

We tend to imagine emotional health as arriving at a place where difficult feelings no longer touch us — where we've engineered our way out of the system altogether. But that's not how any core emotional circuit works, grief included. Health isn't the absence of the signal. It's a working relationship with it: less shame, more tolerance for big feelings, and more willingness to let a system like Panic/Grief, Fear, or Rage tell you something important instead of rushing to shut it down.

Nan and Jilly happy together
Source: photo by Nan Wise

My husband walked into a vet's office with a box of foam steps, and five strangers briefly let one core system do its job in each other's company. That's not a small thing. It might be the clearest argument I know for why understanding these systems — all of them, not just the ones that feel comfortable to feel or talk about — is the work that matters.

item.title: What to Do if You're the Target of a Smear Campaign
item.description:
Trauma

What to Do if You're the Target of a Smear Campaign

Being the target of a smear campaign can feel like psychological and emotional warfare.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Being the target of a smear campaign can be terrifying.
  • Smear campaigns are attempts to influence and control how people perceive a person.
  • Never lose your sense of self during a smear campaign.
  • Ignore the smears when possible and defend yourself when necessary.

Being the target of a smear campaign can feel like psychological and emotional warfare. The injustice, the cruelty, the fabrications, the distortions, and the unwarranted and unfair attacks on your character and reputation can feel intimidating and terrifying. They are most often associated with politics and the celebrity world, but they can also take place in communities, families, and within interpersonal relationships (Samoilenko et al, 2016). A smear campaign may feel like the end of a career, relationship, or friendship and make a person feel unsafe and insecure, but it can also be a beginning if the target can stay true to themselves throughout the ordeal.

A smear campaign is defined as acts by a person or a group of people to discredit or socially harm another person by spreading lies, misinformation, or false allegations about that person. It is often a sustained attempt to influence how people perceive or view an individual. These campaigns are often commenced without the victim’s knowledge, and they can have a devastating impact on their life and relationships.

Smear campaigns are a form of psychological and emotional abuse and can also be linked to narcissistic abuse, coercive control, and domestic abuse. They are linked to these forms of abuse as the intention is often to have power and control over how the targeted person is viewed by other people and, in turn, how they are treated socially. The impact can be that the target is socially isolated, rejected, and ostracised (Reiser, 2024). Some people may believe the smears and character attacks, and that can be humiliating, socially isolating, and degrading to the person being targeted (Kabatova, 2026).

I have been the subject of a smear campaign, and I have also helped people who are going through one. I believe the best thing to do is to know yourself, defend yourself when necessary, and be discerning about what you engage with. Not every false allegation or lie told about you requires your time and energy. Protect yourself when necessary, but do not engage or entertain the campaign if you can. If the campaign is happening online, try and ignore the content as much as possible. This can be very difficult when the natural impulse is to defend and protect yourself and your reputation.

Celebrities are often subjected to smear campaigns, and their humiliation is often played out on an international scale on social media and through the press, where the stakes can be much higher. Some people find the psychological and emotional torture to be too much, and people have ended their own lives as a consequence. There are many reasons why someone might be a target of a smear campaign, ranging from domestic or narcissistic abuse to competition, jealousy, contempt, betrayal and political rivalry. This article is my attempt to help those who wish to recover, move on, and not only survive a smear campaign but thrive after one.

Here are five things that may help you to navigate a smear campaign:

  1. Pay attention to anyone who believes the smears and supports those attacking your character, and take steps to distance yourself from them when possible. If someone is willing to believe falsehoods about you, then it can be inferred that they are not someone who supports and genuinely cares for you. Other people may be gullible and believe the stories, and if that is the case, a simple conversation should help clear the air and set the record straight. Anyone who knows you well will most likely not give credibility or respect to any lies or fabrications told about you. Smear campaigns can help you to see who your true friends and allies are.
  2. If you can starve the campaign of any power and influence, do that. Defend yourself if necessary, e.g., in legal proceedings or in serious cases. To defend yourself, remain calm, collect evidence, get appropriate support and avoid altercations and arguments if possible. But if you can ignore the attacks and smears, that is the best course of action. Today’s gossip and rumours will often be forgotten by most people tomorrow, as by then they will most likely be thinking and talking about something else and somebody else. Weather the storm by taking shelter when possible; nonsense does not always require your participation or energy. Preserve your dignity and do not engage if possible; this can be hard for many people. It is natural to want to defend yourself and set things straight, but this may add fuel to the fire if not done appropriately.
  3. Happy, healthy, and thriving people do not begin or engage in smear campaigns. Consider why someone might start a smear campaign and acknowledge the time, effort, and commitment that it takes to try to smear someone. The fact that it is happening is evidence that the person most likely perceives or considers you to be a threat to them. This should serve as a sign for you to avoid this person and avoid confronting them. Understanding the motivations of people who do this should help you to understand why it is happening. A person who behaves in this way is not healthy or happy with themselves, and their behaviour is highlighting that problem.
  4. Seek help and support from people whom you trust and who can hold space for you while you process what is happening. Being smeared and having your character attacked, especially by someone who was once close to and trusted, can be traumatic, painful, and scary. You do not have to suffer in silence, and there will be people who can help you recover. A good, compassionate friend and some therapists can help, too. I support people recovering from domestic abuse and narcissistic abuse, and many of those people have been subjected to smear campaigns. It may feel like the end of the world, but always remember “this too shall pass.”
  5. The most important thing to do is never abandon or lose your sense of self. Stay connected to yourself and remember who you are, and do not allow other people to manipulate and gaslight you to the point where they take control of your mind, your thoughts, your feelings and your sense of self. If someone is smearing you, it is because you matter to them and they want to control you. You can take your power back by focusing on things you can control. You know who you are, and that is what is most important.

I hope this has been helpful, and if you are the subject of a smear campaign and feel hopeless, helpless, confused, and alone, please seek help and support. A smear campaign is an attempt to control, discredit and influence how other people see you, but they often don’t succeed, and they will end. Always remember, what other people say or think about you is not your business, but what you do with your life and time is your responsibility, so choose wisely. Starve any character attacks of all their power by focusing on your actions and future and ignoring anyone or anything that tries to pull you down. That is how you will thrive after a smear campaign.

item.title: The Case of the Projected Grandmother
item.description:
Social Life

The Case of the Projected Grandmother

It’s reassuring, but not surprising, that the dead tend to agree with us.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Social projection brings perceptions of self-other similarity.
  • Projection works regardless of whether the others are dead or alive.
  • We do not know whether the dead would want us to project on them.

My ancestor disagrees with your ancestor. —Hoca Camide, trying to leverage rhetoric

According to Chinese mythology, we die twice. First, there’s the end to our physical existence; then, there comes the time when the last person who knew us in this world comes to join us in the other. Yet, the dead have a way of asserting themselves, or rather, our mind-brains have ways of keeping the dead in play. Some individuals are remembered and talked about for millennia. Achilles’ mother told her son that eternal fame was an option for him; if he chose it, though, he’d have to die young in war.

And then there’s Odysseus, conjured back to life by Mr. Nolan and his film crew. Odysseus himself, in the epic and in the movie, does Nolan one better. He conjures the dead from Hades and talks to them. The mythologically naïve may assume that Odysseus actually had questions, and that the dead actually had answers. The psychologist, however, assumes that it was all in Odysseus’s head to begin with. Tiriseas, the blind seer, being dead, could only be an imaginary vehicle to bring Odysseus’s own thoughts to light.

This is not as irrational as it may sound. Odysseus, or someone in his shoes, may be aware that most of the contents of his mind are not accessible, but that with proper stimulation, images and insights can emerge. The dead are part of the internal audience to whom we play in our everyday behavior. When a desired goal is finally reached, we say to each other and to ourselves that Grandma would have been proud. Indeed, there is a line just like that in the Odyssey movie, but I forget who says it to whom.

In the world as it exists, the applause of others is a matter of numbers. Its utility, that is, the pleasure we derive from it, increases as more people clap, though each additional clapper adds less to our enjoyment than the one before. Imaginary applause from the dead is an odd thing because it can work only if we deceive ourselves into thinking they really do care. Otherwise, the imagined gratification of the deceased is a form of consoling self-talk—which is not nothing; it goes as far as it goes.

Thankfully, what occurs with less frequency is imagined reprobation by the dead. “What? You didn’t do your own oil change? As your grandpa, I am so disappointed.” Both the good and the bad words put into the mouths of the dead are projections. They are expressions of our beliefs. By attributing these beliefs to someone else who cannot dispute them, they bring to awareness our own beliefs and, with repetition, these projections solidify that which we consider to be true.

The psychological research on social projection has a long history, and I dedicated a good part of my career to figuring out the mental mechanisms in play (Krueger, 1998). Much of the work at the time was concerned with the question of accuracy. Does social projection degrade or improve social perception? Mostly, the latter seems to be the case. As most people are cut from the same human cloth, they share many similarities in their outlook, a result that is reinforced by local culture and the general preference for homophily (liking to hang out with the like-minded). Most of the dead we care about were liked ones and loved ones, members of our social circles of collective cognition. When they come to mind and speak up, it’s no surprise that what they say is no surprise. It’s what we want to hear, or, at least, what we are prepared to hear.

In a creative recent extension of projection research, André Mata, Francisco Cruz, and Rosário Ferreira invited their Portuguese participants to bring to mind a close and deceased person, such as a beloved avó (grandma) and estimate what their opinion might be on an issue of interest. Critically, the researchers had nudged the participants’ own attitude using a standard priming method. This made for a strong test of the projection hypothesis. Not only could it be shown that within an experimental condition, participants’ self-reported attitudes predicted the attitudes attributed to avó, but in one of the two experiments, the data showed that grandma’s attitude had shifted along with the participants’ as if grandma herself had undergone the attitude-change manipulation.

Notice that the question of accuracy does not arise here. Who knows what grandma really believed? With accuracy off the table, this experiment shows with stark clarity that the perception of self-other similarity is a matter of projection instead of introjection. To claim it had been the latter, one would have to assume that, indeed, grandma’s attitude down in Hades was changed by the circumstances prevailing in the lab, and that the participants then aligned their attitudes with what they felt grandma would want. This hypothesis is a bit too far out to be taken seriously.

Why do people project to the dead? Several mini-motives come to mind: Projection is easy, it feels good, it gives a sense of validity to one’s own opinions, and it reinforces the bond with a formerly significant person. So, there really is no good hypothesis on the table that says it should be otherwise. On this, we can count on the dead’s consent. They have always known this to be true.

item.title: When Infinity Breaks the Scale
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

When Infinity Breaks the Scale

AI may create a kind of abundance that challenges how we measure difference.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • AI can make output soar while human effort shrinks toward zero.
  • Old yardsticks like size and headcount start to lose their meaning.
  • The interesting question is where difference goes when the metrics fail.
Source: Faizal Sugi / Pixabay

Indulge me in a little mathematics. Brian Solis and Dave Wright recently introduced the idea of the “Infinite Company,” a provocative way of thinking about organizations built around artificial intelligence (AI). And as a bit of a math geek, I couldn't resist taking this idea down another rabbit hole, and I began to wonder what happens if we take it a little more literally.

When the Denominator Approaches Zero

Typically, we describe AI through the language of exponential change that yields more—more intelligence, greater productivity, expanding capability and capacity. But consider a simple equation where organizational leverage equals output divided by human effort. AI can increase the output while simultaneously reducing the human effort required to produce it. As that denominator gets progressively smaller and approaches zero, the ratio doesn't simply become very large. Mathematically, it begins heading toward infinity. Conceptually a bit abstract, but stay with me.

Of course, no company will operate with literally zero human effort. People (at least for now) still provide intention, judgment, capital, responsibility, and direction, while AI itself requires enormous infrastructure and energy. So maybe the denominator never gets anywhere close to zero, and perhaps organizational leverage remains perfectly measurable. But this is a thought experiment, and it may be pushing the mathematics harder than the economics will permit or even tolerate. Still, following it toward the limit (as the denominator gets closer to zero) exposes something curious about measurement itself.

So, and much to the horror of many, let's do some math. Imagine two concentric circles, one larger than the other. The larger circle has a greater circumference, so common sense suggests that it must contain more points along a larger surface. However, both circles actually contain infinitely many points, and they contain the same number of points. Here's how this makes sense. Draw a line from their common center through the smaller circle and continue it outward, and every point on the smaller circle can be paired with a point on the larger one. The circles remain obviously different in size, but along this particular mathematical dimension, their infinities are equivalent. (You might want to sketch out this description to get a better sense of it.)

A couple of years ago, I explored infinity as a way of thinking about AI’s seemingly boundless possibilities. Today, it's worth another look for a different reason. Perhaps infinity doesn't simply expand possibility, but under certain conditions, it can also make comparison itself more difficult.

Now bring this curiosity back to AI. Two companies can remain profoundly different in revenue, influence, capital, and consequence while their ratio of output to human effort moves toward the same mathematical boundary. They haven't become equal. The problem is with the ruler we chose to compare them. At the limit, infinity destroys the metric that produced it.

The Failure of Comparison

Beyond abstract mathematics, I think this is important because human judgment depends heavily on comparison. We understand much of the world through relative measures such as bigger and smaller, faster and slower, expert and novice. These scales give structure to judgment.

Here's where it gets interesting. AI may create forms of abundance that make some of those scales harder to interpret. If almost everyone has access to extraordinary computational intelligence, having “more intelligence” may tell us progressively less. If one person can summon productive capacity once associated with hundreds of employees, headcount becomes a weaker proxy for organizational power. And—the key point—if key business components like words, images, analyses, and strategies can be produced almost without limit, the sheer quantity may tell us surprisingly little about value.

Perhaps none of this means the metrics actually disappear. We can still do the "business math" and count employees, measure productivity, and calculate market value. The stranger possibility is that the numbers continue to work while the distinctions behind them become less meaningful. The ruler hasn't broken. We may simply be measuring the wrong thing.

Where Does the Difference Go?

This is where the thought experiment gets uncomfortable, at least for me. If abundance compresses some of the differences we have traditionally relied upon, difference doesn't disappear—it moves. We then have to find it somewhere else and create a new metric for today's infinite companies.

Could it migrate? Maybe it moves toward a more human frame that can include judgment, intention, originality, trust, responsibility, or taste. And that uncertainty may be more important than choosing the next set of metrics too quickly. We have spent much of the AI era asking how much more intelligence, productivity, and capability these systems can produce. Those are natural questions because they fit comfortably on scales we already understand and are very comfortable with.

Infinity introduces a different problem. Two circles can remain unmistakably different while becoming identical under one way of counting them. AI may eventually create a similar confusion between capability and value, or between production and meaning.

The numbers may continue getting larger. The more interesting moment will come when we realize that getting larger—and perhaps even abundance itself—no longer tells us what we thought it did.
